newsitem.title: USA: Rubin says balanced U.S. budget within reach.
newsitem.headline: Rubin says balanced U.S. budget within reach.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Tuesay that success in reducing the deficit has bolstered the U.S. economy and brought a balanced federal budget within reach.
"We are in strong economic shape today and and within striking distance of balancing the budget," Rubin said in testimony prepared for delivery to the tax-writing House ways and means committee.
He said a reduced federal deficit has inspired business confidence and driven down interest rates, in turn sustaining an ongoing expansion in economic activity.

Rubin, just back from a weekend meeting in Berlin with counterparts from other Group of Seven industrial nations, said there was broad recognition there that the United States has regained its position as the world's economic leader.

"In fact, the United States now has the best economic conditions among all of the developed major industrial nations," he said, but added that further, steady deficit reduction was critical to maintain the momentum.
He said the Clinton administration's fiscal 1998 budget proposals, which foresee budget balance by 2002, use "real numbers and no gimmicks" to reach that goal.

Rubin said the administration was making "tough choices" to reach the objective of balance between government spending and income, but insisted it was preferable to pursue the goal of balancing the budget in that way rather than by setting a constitutional requirement to do so.
He said a legally mandated balanced budget amendment "is a threat to our economic health and should not be adopted.
"Such an amendment will not make for us the tough policy choices that we ourselves must make to balance the budget, and it will subject our economy to unacceptable risks," Rubin said.

The Treasury chief said difficult issues must be addressed in the budget debate, including "long-term entitlement problems due to demographic trends such as the aging of the baby boomers," and he urged bipartisan cooperation to do so.

Rubin repeated that it was important to provide the resources for the United States to maintain its global leadership as well. He said it was vital to pay America's share to keep international financial institutions healthy.

"To shape world events to advance our security and economic self-interest, we must meet our international obligations and support and lead in the United Nations and in the international financial institutions, such as the World Bank, the International Development Association and the International Monetary Fund," Rubin said.
The United States owes hundreds of millions of dollars in arrears to international institutions including those that lend money for development to poorer countries.
